sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The effectiveness of multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) depends on how collaboration is organized. Many systems rely on fixed collaboration structures with pre-designed agent roles, communication patterns, or workflow components (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Dat et al., 2026). Yet coordination Equal contribution. Project Lead. Corresponding Author. 1 Figure 1: Overall accuracy versus collaboration size. Accuracy versus the mean number of agent roles per question on 688 questions (Qwen3.5-27B). In Forced mode, DynaFlow improves accuracy from Bases 75.9% to 88.1%. Dynamic achieves 87.9% with 3.44 agent roles per question on average, while answering 47% of questions without workflows. requirements vary across tasks: simple queries may need only one agent, independent subtasks can benefit from parallel execution, and dependent stages require reliable access to upstream results. Applying fixed collaboration structure across these settings can introduce unnecessary communication, latency, and computation (Wang et al., 2026; Li and Wang, 2026; Yin et al., 2026). We argue that scalable MAS require stronger capability, which we refer to as Free Orchestration: the ability to decide when collaboration is useful and construct task-specific workflows during problem solving. Automated workflow design has begun to address this rigidity. Existing approaches search for effective workflows using execution feedback (Zhang et al., 2025c), or generate and adapt queryspecific agent systems during inference (Ye et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Tieu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b; Ke et al., 2025, 2026). However, these advances retain constraints on workflow construction and adaptation. DyFlow revises plans using execution feedback but constructs them from finite set of operator templates (Wang et al., 2025b). Figure 2: Overview of DynaFlow. (1) Two-stage SFT trains only the Main Agent on first-turn reasoning and workflow action a1, using distilled demonstrations followed by curated subset. (2) It chooses to answer directly, call tool, or generate JavaScript workflow. (3) Frozen sub-agents collaborate within the workflow according to the Main Agents program. (4) Outputs and execution traces update the history for subsequent decisions. MAS-Orchestra formulates orchestration through function calls, yet generates the complete coordination structure in single decision without observing intermediate execution results (Ke et al., 2026). These limitations motivate combining freeform workflow synthesis with repeated orchestration decisions informed by execution feedback. We therefore investigate executable workflow synthesis as native action of the task-solving agent, alongside ordinary tool use. The same agent decides (i) when to collaborate, (ii) constructs task-specific programs, and (iii) uses their returned outputs and traces to determine how to proceed. To this end, we introduce DynaFlow (Figure 2), framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the task-solving agents action space. We refer to this agent as the main agent, which coordinates sub-agents responsible for executing delegated subtasks. The Main Agent can answer directly, use ordinary tools, or generate task-specific workflow program. Through minimal execution interface, it defines sub-agent responsibilities, sequential or parallel dependencies, and how intermediate outputs are passed, aggregated, and verified directly in code. budget-constrained runtime executes the program and returns its outputs and execution trace. The Main Agent then uses this feedback to guide subsequent actions, including synthesizing follow-up workflows that adapt collaboration to the observed results. We decouple orchestration learning from subagent training by updating only the Main Agent on distilled workflow demonstrations while keeping all sub-agents fixed. This focuses learning on coordinating existing capabilities and allows pretrained models to be reused as executors without retraining. The training process begins with distilled workflow demonstrations. Since answer correctness alone does not guarantee reliable coordination, we then refine the policy on curated subset that excludes demonstrations flagged for unsupported premises, biased verification, or incomplete information transfer. This training process makes orchestration quality an explicit criterion for selecting demonstrations, guiding the Main Agent toward more reliable task coordination and information use. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multihop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline using the same backbone by 10.90 percentage points. In Dynamic mode, it maintains accuracy close to Forced execution while answering 47.1% of questions without invoking workflow. Further analysis finds that training leads to more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs. Together, these results support learning both how to organize collaboration and when to invoke it, and identify cross-stage information use as key dimension of effective orchestration.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic Workflows and Orchestration. workflow specifies model and tool calls through instructions, control flow, and information dependencies. Control flow determines execution order and branching, while data flow specifies which intermediate outputs later calls receive. Orchestra2 tion organizes these calls to solve task. AutoGen provides programmable agent interactions, while Magentic-One and Apodex 1.1 support runtime coordination and replanning (Wu et al., 2024; Fourney et al., 2024; Apodex Team, 2026b). Graphand code-based representations support automated workflow design (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025c), and executable code can express tooluse actions and orchestration logic (Wang et al., 2024; OConnor, 2026). These advances provide expressive mechanisms for collaboration, while verification-centered systems emphasize checking intermediate decisions and their supporting evidence (Apodex Team, 2026a; MiroMind Team, 2026). We therefore focus on learning when to invoke collaboration and how to construct taskspecific workflows that preserve, check, and reuse intermediate results. We further examine how training changes workflow patterns, focusing on stage dependencies and the use, verification, and refinement of intermediate results. Comparing these changes alongside design quality and task accuracy helps characterize the properties of effective orchestration and their relationship to improved performance (Figures 5 and 4; 5.3). Learning Task-Specific Orchestration. Taskspecific orchestration raises two related questions: how to learn workflow generation and how to adapt designs using execution feedback, mechanism also studied in agentenvironment interaction and strategy-guided exploration (MiroMind Team, 2025; Li et al., 2026c). MAS-GPT learns queryspecific system generation through supervised training, while FlowReasoner and Mas-Orchestra use reinforcement learning (Ye et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2026). MAS-Zero revises system designs using intermediate results, and DyFlow plans successive subgraphs using feedback (Ke et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). FlowSteer learns graph-editing policies from canvas feedback (Zhang et al., 2026a). MetaAgent-X further jointly trains designers and executors (Zhang et al., 2026c). DynaFlow integrates free-form executable workflow actions into the task-solving policy, coupling collaboration decisions with workflow construction and subsequent decisions based on execution feedback. Its learning framework explicitly selects demonstrations for orchestration quality and trains only the Main Agent, emphasizing reliable information transfer and independent verification with fixed sub-agents.

sections.title: 3 DynaFlow
sections.content: DynaFlow integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the Main Agents action space. The Main Agent selects whether and how to collaborate, while workflow outputs and execution traces inform subsequent decisions (Figure 2). We formalize this decision process before describing orchestration learning with fixed sub-agents.

sections.title: 3.1 Free-Form Workflow Orchestration
sections.content: Given question and task instruction I, the Main Agent follows policy πθ over three action forms: = Atool {Aans, (P, (P ))}, (1) where Atool is the set of ordinary tool-call actions, Aans denotes final-answer output action, and (P, (P )) denotes single workflow action comprising both the JavaScript program synthesized by the Main Agent and its invocation through the workflow tool . Answer content and arguments for ordinary tools are generated with the corresponding actions and left implicit in the notation. At turn k, the Main Agent generates ak πθ( I, q, hk1), where hk1 is the ordered history of previous actions and observations. The same policy therefore decides whether to answer, use tool, or construct and invoke workflow in light of the task and available feedback. We evaluate this policy under two execution modes. In Dynamic mode, the first decision selects between direct answer and workflow call; in Forced mode, the first substantive action must invoke workflow. Forced execution evaluates workflow construction without the initial routing decision. Both modes allow subsequent tool calls and follow-up workflows. Once workflow is invoked, the Main Agent is restricted to coordination and summarization, with substantive problem solving delegated to sub-agents. The program defines sub-agent roles, stages, and dependencies through agent calls, parallel execution, and optional phase labels. Independent calls can run concurrently, while dependent calls receive upstream outputs explicitly. Each sub-agent receives only the instructions and inputs specified by . The workflow tool executes with fixed sub-agents under resource constraints, returning an observation ok = (P ) that combines the program output with an execution trace recording the status and output of each sub-agent call (Figure 2, panel 3; Appendix B). 3 After receiving ok, the Main Agent appends (ak, ok) to the history to obtain hk and generates its next action conditioned on I, q, and hk. When it judges the available information sufficient to answer q, it emits Aans and terminates; otherwise, it invokes tool or workflow to verify, refine, or extend the available results (Figure 2, panel 4). Algorithm 1 summarizes this feedback loop over the action space in Eq. 1.

sections.title: 3.2 Learning the Orchestration Policy
sections.content: Building on the action formulation in 3.1, we train the Main Agent policy πθ to construct taskspecific workflows and coordinate information flow across sub-agents. Training proceeds in two stages, updating only the Main Agent while keeping all sub-agents fixed (Figure 2, panel 1). Stage 1: trajectory distillation. teacher model generates trajectories using the same workflow interface, tools, and fixed sub-agents. We retain trajectories with correct final answers that follow the delegation protocol in 3.1, with substantive solving performed inside workflows. The supervised target = (r, a1) is the Main Agents first-turn output, where is its reasoning and a1 = (P, (P )) is the workflow action defined in 3.1. This yields dataset D1 of examples (I, q, s). Both training stages minimize LSFT(θ; D) = (cid:88) (I,q,s)D log πθ(r, a1 I, q), (2) with = D1 in Stage 1 and the curated subset D2 in Stage 2. The loss supervises both the reasoning tokens in and the action tokens in a1; instructions, questions, and tool definitions are masked. Supervision thus targets first-turn task analysis and workflow synthesis. Stage 2: high-quality data selection. Stage 1 demonstrations meet the final-answer correctness and execution-protocol criteria while varying in orchestration quality. Evaluation of the Stage 1 model reveals that failures in information transfer and incorrect Main Agent judgments can steer workflows toward wrong answers. These observations motivate selecting high-quality demonstrations that support reliable information transfer and independent problem solving within workflows, with the aim of improving the Main Agents orchestration capability. sections.title: 5.1 Overall Performance
sections.content: DynaFlow achieves the highest overall accuracy, reaching 88.08% in Forced mode and 87.94% in Dynamic mode  (Table 1)  . Both exceed the strongest baseline by over 10 percentage points and outperform their Base counterparts, with only the Main Agent trained and all sub-agents fixed. Mathematical reasoning. DynaFlow achieves the strongest results across competition and multilingual mathematics. Forced execution solves all 90 AIME questions, achieving 100% across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 sets, while both modes exceed the strongest baseline on PolyMATH by 34 percentage points. We analyze the generated workflows and find that they organize mathematical solving around complementary derivation, computation, and verification stages. sections.title: 5.2 Effect of Training and Execution Mode
sections.content: We examine how training affects workflow-based solving under matched execution settings (Table 2; Figure 3). Base, Forced underperforms Base, Direct on every benchmark except HotpotQA, where workflows enable retrieval. After Stage 1, Forced execution reaches or exceeds the Base, Direct reference on all six benchmarks and surpasses Direct within the same checkpoint by 8.73 points overall, including retrieval gains on HotpotQA. We thus find that orchestration training turns workflow access into effective collaboration, yielding gains beyond the trained Main Agents standalone performance. This pattern is consistent with prior findings that collaboration benefits depend on task characteristics and coordination structure (Kim et al., 2026). Stage 2 further improves both Forced and Dynamic performance. Our workflow analysis finds higher design quality and more frequent use and refinement of upstream results with fewer sub-agents on average than Stage 1 (Figures 4 and 5; 5.3), linking the performance gains to more focused coordination.

sections.title: Organization
sections.content: Connected stages and improved information use. Figure 5(a,c) shows that Base typically delegates to single sub-agent or constructs calls without dependencies, whereas trained programs usually combine parallel and sequential stages. Hybrid workflows increase from 3.4% for Base to 83.2% after Stage 1 and 85.6% after Stage 2. The share of programs that pass upstream outputs and explicitly instruct downstream agents to use them rises from 12.6% for Base to 93.3% after Stage 1 and 97.7% after Stage 2 (Figure 5(d)). Training thus improves information use in workflow design: the Main Agent increasingly specifies how intermediate results should inform subsequent solving and verification, enabling systematic reuse across stages. Higher-quality information flow and verification. Our analysis of Stage 1 errors identifies three recurring patterns: unsupported premises introduced by the Main Agent, verification guided toward an expected conclusion, and incomplete or incorrect transfer of intermediate information. These observations motivate selecting Stage 2 demonstrations that avoid premise injection, verification defects, and information-flow defects (3.2). After training on the selected data, we find higher proportions of defect-free workflows across all four design criteria. Major information-flow defects decline from 1.9% in Stage 1 to 0.9% in Stage 2 (Figure 4), while workflows that specify correction or refinement of intermediate results increase from 28.1% to 35.9% (Figure 5(e)). We interpret Bases relatively high logical-continuity scores in light of its simpler, often single-agent workflows, which involve fewer dependencies between stages. Task-specific roles and instructions. Figure 6 shows distinct role configurations across tasks. Solvers and verifiers account for over 90% of nodes on AIME and PolyMATH, while researchers account for 59.6% on HotpotQA. GPQA-Diamond combines substantial solver component with more research than the mathematics benchmarks. Verification remains common across tasks, accounting for 33.243.9% of nodes. This task-specific organization extends to the instructions themselves: the Main Agent generates prompt for each subagent that specifies its objective, relevant inputs, and use of upstream results for the current question (3.1). DynaFlow thus adapts both the division of labor and the instructions that guide execution, connecting task decomposition with information use. Relative to the transferred AFlow workflows used in our evaluation (4), this flexibility supports question-specific mathematical derivation, evidence gathering, and independent checking (5.1).

sections.title: 5.4 Adaptive Workflow Invocation
sections.content: The DynamicForced accuracy gap narrows from 10.75 percentage points for Base to 1.02 after Stage 1 and 0.14 for DynaFlow  (Table 2)  . With subagents fixed, this trend highlights the contribution of Main Agent training to selective collaboration. In Dynamic mode, DynaFlow answers 47.1% of questions directly while achieving 87.94% accuracy, close to 88.08% under Forced execution. Averaged over all questions, including those answered directly, it uses 2.44 sub-agents per question versus approximately 4.16 under Forced execution, reduction of about 41% (Figure 1). These results suggest that unified Main Agent policy can adapt its solution strategy to task requirements while maintaining performance with fewer sub-agents. We regard the choice between direct answering and workflow execution as an integral part of orchestration: additional agents do not necessarily improve performance, and collaboration should be invoked according to the needs of each question.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: We view reliable information use alongside task decomposition as central to orchestration; gains with fixed sub-agents support learning to coordinate existing capabilities (5.2). Stage 2 gains accompany better information transfer and more frequent refinement of intermediate results, consistent with screening for unsupported premises, constrained verification, and information-flow defects (5.3). Our analysis of GPQA-Diamond failures illustrates how correct intermediate results can be lost or overridden during verification and final synthesis. DynaFlow workflows incorporate complementary evidence gathering, independent checks, and refinement of intermediate results. Future work could train sub-agents for reliable information transfer and independent verification, and extend first-turn supervision to multi-turn trajectories containing disagreements and erroneous results. Such supervision could strengthen the Main Agents ability to independently assess conflicting outputs, identify errors, and select actions for error recovery, workflow revision, and final-answer selection.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: DynaFlow combines free-form executable workflow actions with two-stage Main Agent training through trajectory distillation and demonstration selection based on orchestration quality, keeping subagents fixed. Across six benchmarks, it achieves 8 the highest overall accuracy among evaluated methods; Dynamic execution answers nearly half the questions directly with accuracy close to Forced execution. Workflow analysis characterizes how training changes structure and the use of intermediate results.

sections.title: A Experimental Setup Details
sections.content: Benchmarks. The evaluation contains 688 questions: 30 from each of AIME 2024, 2025, and 2026; 200 from PolyMATH; 198 from GPQADiamond; and 200 from HotpotQA. PolyMATH and HotpotQA are sampled with seed 42. AIME requires integer answers, PolyMATH includes multilingual mathematical questions with free-form answers, GPQA-Diamond uses multiple-choice scientific questions, and HotpotQA requires connecting evidence across retrieval steps. Models and baselines. The Agent uses Qwen3.527B, and all workflow sub-agents use its Base checkpoint without orchestration training. Both operate with thinking enabled; only the Agent receives orchestration training. CoT, five-sample CoT-SC, Self-Refine, and AFlow use the same backbone. AFlow uses the released MATH workflow on AIME and PolyMATH and the released HotpotQA workflow on HotpotQA and GPQADiamond. These workflows are transferred without an additional workflow search on the evaluation tasks. Base + Web search provides comparison with direct retrieval access.

sections.title: B Workflow Runtime
sections.content: The Main Agent passes JavaScript program to the Workflow tool. Programs define sub-agent instructions and pass intermediate outputs through ordinary code. The interface provides agent for sub-agent calls, parallel for concurrent calls, pipeline for dependent stages over multiple items, and phase for stage labels. sub-agent receives the instruction and inputs specified by the program; the Main Agents interaction history is not automatically inherited. Calls may request structured outputs through JSON schema. Workflow completion returns the program result together with execution information, which the Main Agent can use to revise the workflow or produce final answer. During evaluation, Direct answers without tools, Dynamic selects between direct answering and workflow execution, and Forced requires workflow invocation before substantive problem solving. The corresponding prompts are provided in Appendix F.

sections.title: C Training Details
sections.content: GLM-5.3 Max provides the teacher trajectories. The Stage 1 training set contains 2,257 first-turn demonstrations from HotpotQA and BrowseComp. Supervision covers the first-turn reasoning and action; instructions, questions, and tool definitions are masked from the loss. Only the Main Agent is fine-tuned, while all sub-agents remain fixed. Stage 2 continues from the Stage 1 checkpoint on 712 complete workflow demonstrations selected from the Stage 1 training set: 449 from HotpotQA and 263 from BrowseComp. Both stages train for two epochs using the objective in Eq. (2), with smaller learning rate in Stage 2 and no separate validation split. Table 3 summarizes the training configuration, and Appendix describes data selection. We use ms-swift 4.6.0.dev0 for training with 4-bit NF4 QLoRA, double quantization, BF16 computation, and gradient checkpointing. The Qwen3.5-27B backbone has approximately 27 billion parameters, with 116,727,808 trainable parameters in our configuration. LoRA targets eligible linear layers through all-linear, while the visual encoder and alignment module remain frozen. Each stage runs on two NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with single training process sharding the model across both devices. Based on full job wall-clock time, Stage 1 and Stage 2 consume about 52 and 17 GPU-hours, respectively, totaling about 69 GPUhours. This budget covers fine-tuning only, excluding teacher trajectory generation, evaluation, and LLM-based judging. sections.title: D Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Decoding configuration. Table 4 summarizes the decoding configuration for DynaFlow evaluation. Thinking is enabled for both the Main Agent and sub-agents. The output-token limits apply to individual model responses, rather than the number of workflow stages or interaction turns. 12 unmatched nodes are labeled Other. The Aggregator category covers synthesis, merging, and adjudication. Role proportions are computed over executed sub-agent nodes, with results pooled across the AIME benchmarks.

sections.title: E Orchestration Quality Selection
sections.content: The selection judge is deepseek-flash, with thinking enabled, high reasoning effort, and temperature 0. It receives the question, the workflow program generated in the first turn, and any launch arguments, without the Main Agents reasoning, final answer, reference answer, or execution results. The rubric checks three defects: premise injection, where unsupported answer-relevant claims are supplied as established facts; verification defects, where instructions or output constraints favor an expected conclusion or prevent independent correction; and information-flow defects, where missing context, incorrect references, or substituted values prevent required information from reaching downstream agents. The judge cites excerpts from the workflow program or launch arguments to support each reported defect. We verify these excerpts against the supplied text as part of the quality screening. From the 2,254 workflow-containing demonstrations, we retain 712 complete first-turn examples for Stage 2.

sections.title: Interface
sections.content: Figure 7 presents concise versions of the Direct, Dynamic, and Forced evaluation prompts, the shared answer format, and the Workflow tool interface. These prompts specify the conditions for workflow invocation, task delegation, and use of returned results. The Main Agent determines subagent roles, instructions, and workflow structure for each question. Repeated formatting instructions are omitted for brevity.

Answer scoring. For DynaFlow, the prediction is extracted from the Main Agents final FINAL ANSWER line; intermediate reasoning and sub-agent outputs are not substituted for an absent final answer. Runs without valid final answer are counted as incorrect. AIME answers are matched as integers after normalizing leading zeros, and GPQADiamond answers are matched to the questions option labels. PolyMATH permits exact mathematical equivalence, while HotpotQA accepts answers that identify the reference entity or relation, including equivalent names and aliases. Approximate decimals are not accepted as exact answers when the task specifies no numerical precision. Workflow quality and structure. Workflow programs generated in Forced mode are evaluated by deepseek-flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) with thinking enabled, high reasoning effort, and temperature 0, using the question and program without execution results. Task consistency, decomposition appropriateness, logical continuity, and informationflow correctness are scored as 0 (major defect), 1 (minor weakness), or 2 (no defect). sections.title: Shared task and answer format
sections.content: The task supplies question and task identifier, with optional attachment names or paths. Before the final answer, output record: {"task_id": "<task_id>", "Final answer": "<final_answer>"} If no task identifier is supplied, use an empty string. Finish the response with: FINAL ANSWER: [YOUR FINAL ANSWER] Follow the answer format requested by the task and do not include explanations after this final line. Workflow: delegation and tool interface Task delegation. Provide the original task, relevant context, attachment paths, and output requirements. Design the Workflow for the current task, using sub-agents, parallelism, verification, and additional stages as appropriate. Read and follow the tool description and input schema before invocation. Invocation. Supply JavaScript program through script, or stored program through scriptPath, with optional args. Each script begins with literal meta object containing name and description; optional phases describe its stages. The tool starts execution in the background and returns task identifier; completion notification provides the programs returned result. Execution primitives. agent(prompt, options) launches sub-agent and returns final text or validated object when JSON schema is supplied. parallel(thunks) runs calls concurrently and waits for their results. pipeline(items, stages...) processes each item through dependent stages without waiting for unrelated items. phase(title) labels stage, and args exposes invocation inputs. Ordinary JavaScript passes and transforms intermediate outputs in an asynchronous context. Result handling. Do not independently duplicate the Workflows problem solving in the Main Agent. If results are incomplete, uncertain, or contradicted by evidence, revise or rerun the Workflow. Answer only when the returned results are sufficient, and base the final answer on them. Report failure if Workflow is unavailable or cannot complete. Figure 7: Evaluation prompts and Workflow interface. sections.title: H Case Studies of Workflow Changes
sections.content: We compare selected Base and DynaFlow workflows under Forced execution with fixed sub-agents, complementing the analysis of information use and task-specific organization in 5.3. Each diagram is reconstructed from the workflow program and execution record; captions specify the displayed invocation and distinguish executed calls from conditional branches. Complementary computation and explicit verification. For the palindrome-counting problem from AIME 2026 (Figure 8), Base delegates to one solver, which returns 59 after an arithmetic error. DynaFlow assigns enumeration, dynamic programming, and inclusionexclusion to parallel solvers, then passes their outputs to verifier for comparison and independent recomputation. All three solvers and the verifier obtain 62. This case illustrates how complementary methods and explicit use of intermediate results support mathematical verification. Preserving research evidence for scientific adjudication. For the reaction-product question from GPQA-Diamond (Figure 9), Base runs two analyses sequentially without passing results between them. DynaFlow assigns four research calls to distinct chemical constraints and checks the candidate products for each reaction. Both checks challenge their initial candidates, and the decision agent receives the research evidence alongside the verification results. Preserving these complementary inputs enables final synthesis to account for both the proposed answers and the objections raised during verification. Connecting entity identification to subsequent retrieval. For the HotpotQA question requiring person identification and year retrieval (Figure 10), the displayed Base call searches for investment firms and their founding years. DynaFlow instead uses three search routes to identify candidate entities, deduplicates and ranks them, and passes their names, quotations, and sources to candidatespecific resolution agents. Subsequent checks assess the selected proposal. This organization connects retrieval steps through explicit intermediate entities and supporting evidence, as discussed in 5.1. Linking solution stages to audits and conditional repair. For the geometric optimization problem Figure 8: AIME 2026: palindrome counting. Base uses one solver; DynaFlow connects three complementary computations to common verifier. The dashed retry branch was not triggered. Repeated input and result packaging is omitted. For person candidates, resolution prompts prioritize birth-year retrieval. 18 Figure 11: AIME 2025: geometric optimization. Base shows its second invocation; DynaFlow shows its first. The starred optimizer was excluded before fitting because it returned no valid output. Both audits confirmed the candidate, so the dashed conditional repair call was not executed. 19 bility. DynaFlow addresses these challenges at the agent-workflow level by selectively invoking collaboration, explicitly organizing dependencies, and training the Main Agent on demonstrations filtered for orchestration quality. Positioning of DynaFlow. DynaFlow unifies task-specific workflow synthesis, adaptive collaboration decisions, and feedback-driven orchestration within single policy. Unlike methods that optimize fixed workflows or separately train multiple agents, DynaFlow updates only the Main Agent while keeping sub-agents fixed. Its emphasis on explicit information transfer and independent verification enables flexible collaboration tailored to individual tasks.

sections.title: I Extended Related Work
sections.content: Multi-Agent Collaboration and Orchestration. LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have progressed from predefined role-based collaboration toward adaptive, task-specific orchestration. Early approaches establish structured interactions through specialized agents, communication protocols, and iterative reasoning (Chen et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). Recent methods further explore dynamic agent selection, communication topology optimization, and automatic workflow construction (Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026b). Similar principles of specialization and selective information integration have been explored in multimodal learning, including cross-spectral augmentation (Tan et al., 2024b), modality-decoupled representations (Feng et al., 2025a), sparse mixtureof-experts (Feng et al., 2025b), attention-guided alignment (Tan et al., 2026), and dynamic crossmodal coordination (Lin et al., 2026). Unlike approaches relying on predetermined collaboration structures, DynaFlow learns to synthesize executable workflows according to individual task requirements and adapt subsequent decisions using execution feedback. Efficiency and Reliable Information Flow. Effective collaboration requires balancing reasoning quality, computational efficiency, and reliable information exchange. AgentPrune reduces redundant communication (Zhang et al., 2025a), while broader MAS efficiency studies investigate topology optimization and resource allocation (Li et al., 2026a). Meanwhile, analyses of multi-agent failures highlight challenges involving task decomposition, information propagation, and verification (Cemri et al., 2025).

sections.title: Related research has explored robust
sections.content: information selection through saliency-guided transfer (Tan et al., 2024a), semantic label verification (Zhang et al., 2025d), uncertainty-guided expert selection (Zhang et al., 2025e), and generalization-preserving or collaborative continual learning (Zhang et al., 2025f, 2026b). Reliable evidence integration and structured information dependencies also arise in multimodal hallucination mitigation (Shu et al., 2026), dense video correspondence (Wu et al., 2026), and constrained visual generation (Wu et al., 2025). These studies highlight complementary aspects of information selection, coordination, and relia-
